summary: Follow-up to the 2026-04-12 production incident where inference latency spiked and a portion of requests hit degraded model variants. Root cause discussed: rapid traffic burst + cold KV cache + autoscaler cooldown + a misconfigured fallback policy. Short-term mitigations agreed: increase min replicas, adjust cooldowns, warm KV cache, lock fallback to same-size variant. Medium-term: autoscaler tuning, expanded canary, and better QoS routing. Action items assigned and next steps scheduled.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-04-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Redwood CSM), James Rivers (Cobalt CTO), Lena Ortiz (Cobalt SRE), Markus Voss (Platform Eng), Priya Shah (Security)

Summary (auto): Brief recap of incident on 2026-04-12, RCA discussion, immediate mitigations, plan for long-term reliability improvements and compliance follow-up.

Topics: RCA, autoscaler behavior, KV cache warming, fallback policies, SOC2/KMS questions, P0->P1 mitigations, scheduling canary/testing.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Sofia: hey everyone thanks for joining, i think we have about 45 minutes, we'll go through the timeline quick then talk mitigations and next steps
[00:12] James: thanks, appreciate you all. we got paged friday and basically 30% of requests had 3-5x latency and some 503s, customers saw errors in our chat product
[00:25] Arjun: quick note - from our telemetry it looked like there was a sudden traffic burst, autoscaler didn't catch up because of cooldown and a bunch of lanes ended up falling back to smaller model variants, plus KV cache coldness added token generation overhead
[00:45] Lena: that's right, our logs show many cache misses around 13:02 UTC and the fallback policy sent those to a quantized variant which is slightly incompatible with prompt features - that's why a subset returned garbled structured outputs
[01:05] Markus: just to be clear, when you say fallback - is that the policy that switches to a smaller model when latency target is missed? we thought that fallback should preserve model family
[01:18] Arjun: yeah our config allowed fallback across family boundaries for capacity reasons; that was explicit in the rollout config but we didn't realize downstream prompts required tokenizer parity. doesn't help that the transcriber sometimes says 'redwood privat' in notes, our docs call it Redwood Private.
[01:37] James: there were also some mis-encoded tokens in the transcript that made our pipelines reject responses, so we had an error cascade.
[01:47] Sofia: ok, so root causes summarized: burst traffic + autoscaler not scaling fast enough + cooldown settings too long + KV cache not warmed + fallback to incompatible variant. does that match?
[02:02] Priya: we also want to confirm encryption in transit was unaffected, our security team reviewed and saw no broken TLS or KMS operations, just the data quality issues
[02:15] Maya: i pulled the SOC2 artifact snapshots you'll need, and i'll share the KMS rotation notes, safe to send those docs to the security mailbox?
[02:26] Priya: yes send to sec-requests@cobalt.com, we'll ingest and index.
[02:30] Arjun: immediate mitigations we proposed during the incident were: roll back the fallback policy to same-family variants, increase min replicas for the dedicated pool, shorten autoscaler cooldown threshold for bursty signals, and perform a KV cache warming after deploy.
[02:46] Lena: we did an interim config change that bumped min replicas but the cooldown was still biting us at the peak, so we want a proactive approach: predictive scaling and pre-warming before expected bursts
[03:02] James: can you outline which of these are config-only vs code deploys? we want the low-risk things first
[03:12] Arjun: sure - config-only: fallback restriction, min replicas bump, cooldown tweak. code deploy: predictive autoscaler that uses rate-of-change signal and the cache-warming hook in the runtime - that needs a patch to the autoscaler controller and will take a bit longer.
[03:30] Sofia: okay we agreed to do the low-risk config changes as a canary in staging this week then promote to prod with a short maintenance window, is that correct?
[03:39] Lena: correct, staging first. we'll also run a traffic replay to validate.
[03:45] Markus: one suggestion - can we have a canary policy that keeps the KV cache warmed for a small percentage of traffic? like a continuous micro-warm strategy?
[03:56] Arjun: yes that's feasible, we can add a warming worker that issues prefixes to keep KV hot. there's a small cost but negligible compared to a full cold start.
[04:07] Priya: security question: when you adjust min replicas does that change our data residency guarantees or logging? we need to ensure audit logs still show key access and tenant separation
[04:18] Maya: no, min replicas is purely compute; KMS and audit logging are unaffected. i'll share the exact audit log example we collected during the incident.
[04:28] James: also timeline - what will you send us today and what do you need from us?
[04:33] Sofia: we'll send the incident timeline, anonymized logs, and a list of the config changes we propose. we need your SRE to run a replay on staging and confirm acceptance criteria: 95th p99 latency below X ms and zero structured output errors for 10k messages across the replay.
[04:55] Lena: ok we'll try to run that by friday, want to coordinate time with Arjun for the environment snapshot
[05:03] Arjun: i'll prepare the snapshot and the config diff. also note: we recommend toggling the fallback to same-family and enabling per-route circuit breakers so a noisy route won't cascade to others
[05:18] James: do you have any recommendations for batching parameters? we noticed spikes correlate with short chat sessions with many small requests
[05:28] Arjun: yes, small requests are tricky. we can enable micro-batching with a short hold window (10-20ms) to capture aggregation without increasing tail latency too much. also per-customer batching could help.
[05:43] Sofia: there was a question about mitigation scope - is this specific to Dedicated pools or also relevant to Hosted?
[05:52] Arjun: both. hosters with dynamic multitenant pools will see similar issues if fallback policies are mis-configured or KV cache is cold. Dedicated customers have control over min replicas so fix is easier there, hosted customers rely on our runtime defaults.
[06:10] Priya: on the compliance side we need a short writeup showing when keys were used during incident and the rotation history
[06:18] Maya: i'll include that in the package.
[06:22] James: what's the rollback plan if the canary shows regressions? we can't afford another outage during the weekend
[06:29] Arjun: rollback plan: quick revert of config via infra pipeline, restore autoscaler settings to previous thresholds, and if needed pin traffic to stable region or smaller tenant pool. we can also force a model-pin on critical routes to avoid fallback variance.
[06:47] Lena: who will run the post-change verification? we will, with Redwood watching and Arjun helping with observability hooks
[06:55] Sofia: ok, check. we'll also add extra alerts for KV miss rate and fallback count so we get early signal.
[07:05] Markus: can we get a short doc that explains model-family fallback safety and tokenizer parity? our platform engineers were surprised that variant changes could affect tokenization
[07:17] Arjun: yes i'll prepare a short tech note - "model-family fallback & tokenizer parity" - that'll include examples and recommended guardrails.
[07:28] James: great. Priya also asked earlier about whether any PII left the system during the incident - can you confirm?
[07:35] Maya: we checked, data retention and encryption were intact, there was no exfil, only degraded outputs, so no PII leakage. we'll send the confirmation in writing.
[07:45] Sofia: ok moving on to timeline items and owners.
[07:50] [15:00 mark omitted - meeting proceeds through technical details, logs references, and config diffs]
[20:12] Arjun: note from the runtime trace - many sessions had repeated cache misses because the prefix encoder includes timestamp metadata, we recommended normalizing prefix structure to increase cache hit rate
[20:30] Lena: yeah we can standardize prefixes in our client side lib, will take a small change to SDK but long term beneficial
[25:00] Sofia: action recap: we'll send artifacts: incident timeline, anonymized logs, proposed config diff, tech note on fallback/tokenizers, SOC2 snapshot. Cobalt will run staging replay and provide pass/fail.
[30:10] James: approximate risk - if we do the config-only changes this week, what's the chance of another regression?
[30:20] Arjun: low to medium - config-only reduces the main risk surface, but predictive autoscaler and warming will be the full solution. we estimate config-only will cut incidents by ~70% for this pattern
[32:05] Priya: can Redwood provide a 24-hour contact for the rollout window? we may want an on-call Redwood SE during the canary promotion
[32:14] Sofia: yes Arjun and I can be on-call for the window, and Maya will handle customer comms.
[33:00] Markus: one more ask - can we run a synthetic workload that mimics the Tuesday spike? we'll share the request trace and you can help orchestrate
[33:10] Arjun: absolutely, we'll help script the replay and share load test parameters.
[34:05] Lena: also we'll collect structured-output error metrics specifically for the tokenization mismatch cases
[34:14] Sofia: good. any other open questions?
[34:20] James: just timeline, recap: send artifacts by 2026-04-20, config canary staged by 2026-04-23, replay and verification by 2026-04-24, full promotion week of 2026-04-27 pending success
[34:38] Maya: noted.
[34:42] Priya: security will review SOC2 artifacts and KMS notes and confirm by 2026-04-22
[35:00] Sofia: ok thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the canary window and the replay session, and post the incident doc in the shared drive
[35:12] James: thanks, appreciate the responsiveness
[35:18] Sofia: meeting adjourned.
[44:30] End of recording.
